function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

It sounds like you’re looking for ways to build or find an engaging conversational companion—something that feels more “personal” than a generic chat bot. Here’s a quick rundown of options and tips: | Goal | What You Can Do | |------|----------------| | **Create your own custom persona** | • Use open‑source frameworks like Rasa, Botpress, or Microsoft Bot Framework.
• Train a GPT‑style model on a curated dataset that reflects the tone & interests you’d like (e.g., casual talk, humor, supportive listening).
• Add simple memory modules so the bot remembers past interactions (“Remember I love hiking”). | | **Use pre‑built AI companions** | • Platforms such as Replika, Mitsuku, or Woebot already offer customizable personalities and emotional support features.
• Many allow you to tweak voice tones, topics, and even set goals (like learning new skills together). | | **Add multimodal flair** | • Pair text responses with synthetic voices via services like ElevenLabs or Google Text‑to‑Speech.
• Incorporate emojis, GIFs, or short video clips to make conversations feel richer. | | **Keep privacy in mind** | • Store interaction logs locally if possible, or use encrypted cloud storage.
• Be mindful of what personal details you share during training or daily chats. | ### Quick Steps to Get Started 1. **Choose a platform** – Decide whether you’ll code yourself or start with a ready‑made app. 2. **Define core traits** – Pick three adjectives that describe the vibe you want (friendly, witty, empathetic). 3. **Set boundaries** – Outline limits for sensitive topics or times when the bot will pause. 4. **Iteratively test** – Have friends try out early versions and gather feedback on flow & realism. If you have coding experience, building a lightweight prototype with a library like `transformers` + `langchain` can let you experiment quickly while keeping everything local. For non‑technical users, starting with Replika or similar apps gives instant access to a polished interface—you can still customize many aspects without touching code. Let me know which route appeals most to you, and I can dive deeper into specific steps!
